entry.sum: The fundamental group $\pi_1(X, x_0)$ records the loops in a space $X$ based at a point $x_0$, where two loops count as the same if one can be continuously deformed into the other with the base point held fixed; joining loops end to end makes these classes a group. Covering spaces, such as the map $\mathbb{R} \to S^1$ that wraps the line around the circle, are the main tool for computing it: lifting loops upstairs turns 'how many times does the loop go round' into an integer, which gives $\pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.
key: p : (\tilde X, \tilde x_0) \to (X, x_0) \text{ a covering map} \;\Longrightarrow\; p_* : \pi_1(\tilde X, \tilde x_0) \to \pi_1(X, x_0) \text{ is injective}
entry.why: It is the first algebraic invariant that can prove two spaces are not homeomorphic (the plane with one hole versus the plane with two holes) and that certain maps cannot exist, which gives short proofs of the two-dimensional Brouwer fixed point theorem and of the fundamental theorem of algebra. Covering spaces and their deck groups also turn up in complex analysis, in Lie theory and in the study of knots.

links.note: The winding number of a closed curve around a point, which governs Cauchy's integral formula and the residue theorem, is exactly the integer that $\pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{a\}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ assigns to the curve.

Loops around a solenoid that cannot be contracted in the field-free region underlie the Aharonov–Bohm effect, and $\pi_1(SO(3)) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ is why a rotation through $2\pi$ cannot be continuously undone while one through $4\pi$ can (the belt trick), the topological root of spin-$\tfrac12$.

blocks.body:
A rubber band lying flat on a table can always be shrunk to a point without lifting it. Loop it around a nail hammered into the table, and it can no longer be shrunk away while it stays on the table: the nail is detected by a loop that cannot be contracted. On a doughnut surface there are two independent such loops, one around the hole and one through it.

The fundamental group turns this into algebra: loops up to continuous deformation, multiplied by doing one after the other. Homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental groups, and continuous maps must respect them. This page assumes [[topological-spaces]] (continuity, path-connectedness, compactness of $[0,1]$) and [[groups]].

blocks.title: Paths, loops and deforming them
blocks.body:
A path in a space $X$ is a continuous map $f : [0,1] \to X$, and a loop based at $x_0$ is a path with $f(0) = f(1) = x_0$.

Two paths $f, g$ with the same endpoints are path homotopic, written $f \simeq g$, if there is a continuous map $F : [0,1] \times [0,1] \to X$ with $F(s, 0) = f(s)$, $F(s, 1) = g(s)$, $F(0, t) = f(0)$ and $F(1, t) = f(1)$ for all $s, t$. Think of $t$ as time in a film: at each moment we see a path $F(\cdot, t)$ with the same endpoints, and the film moves $f$ to $g$.

If $f$ ends where $g$ begins, the product $f \cdot g$ runs through $f$ and then through $g$, each at double speed:
$$(f \cdot g)(s) = \begin{cases} f(2s), & 0 \le s \le \tfrac12, \\ g(2s - 1), & \tfrac12 \le s \le 1, \end{cases}$$
continuous by the pasting lemma. The reverse path is $\bar f(s) = f(1-s)$.

blocks.title: Fundamental group
blocks.body:
Let $x_0 \in X$. The fundamental group $\pi_1(X, x_0)$ is the set of path-homotopy classes $[f]$ of loops based at $x_0$, with the operation $[f][g] = [f \cdot g]$. Its identity is the class of the constant loop $e_{x_0}$ and the inverse of $[f]$ is $[\bar f]$. A path-connected space whose fundamental group is trivial is called simply connected.

In words: loops up to sliding with the base point held fixed, multiplied by concatenation.

blocks.title: Why this is a group, and what it depends on
blocks.body:
Running homotopies $f \simeq f'$ and $g \simeq g'$ side by side shows $f \cdot g \simeq f' \cdot g'$, so the product of classes is well defined. The loops $(f \cdot g) \cdot h$ and $f \cdot (g \cdot h)$ are not equal (one spends half the time on $f$, the other a quarter), but they differ by a reparametrisation, and for any continuous $\varphi : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ fixing $0$ and $1$ the homotopy $F(s,t) = f((1-t)\varphi(s) + t s)$ shows $f \circ \varphi \simeq f$. The same trick gives $e \cdot f \simeq f \simeq f \cdot e$. Finally $f \cdot \bar f$ shrinks to the constant loop: at time $t$, walk along $f$ only as far as $f(1-t)$ and come back. So $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is a group.

Three basic properties:

1. Change of base point. A path $\alpha$ from $x_0$ to $x_1$ gives an isomorphism $[f] \mapsto [\bar\alpha \cdot f \cdot \alpha]$ from $\pi_1(X, x_0)$ to $\pi_1(X, x_1)$, so for path-connected $X$ one writes $\pi_1(X)$.
2. Functoriality. A continuous $h : X \to Y$ with $h(x_0) = y_0$ induces a homomorphism $h_*[f] = [h \circ f]$, with $(k \circ h)_* = k_* \circ h_*$ and $\mathrm{id}_* = \mathrm{id}$. Hence homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic groups.
3. Products. Loops and homotopies in $X \times Y$ are pairs of loops and homotopies, so $\pi_1(X \times Y) \cong \pi_1(X) \times \pi_1(Y)$.

In a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ the straight-line homotopy $F(s,t) = (1-t) f(s) + t\, g(s)$ joins any two paths with the same endpoints, so convex sets are simply connected. (In $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$ it may run through the origin.) Showing that some group is not trivial is the real work, and needs covering spaces.

blocks.title: Covering map
blocks.body:
A continuous surjection $p : E \to B$ is a covering map if every $b \in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ such that $p^{-1}(U)$ is a union of disjoint open sets $V_\alpha$, each of which $p$ maps homeomorphically onto $U$. Such a $U$ is said to be evenly covered, and the $V_\alpha$ are the sheets over $U$.

In words: locally, $E$ looks like a stack of copies of $B$, and $p$ just projects the stack down.

blocks.title: The basic example: the line wrapping round the circle
blocks.body:
Let $p : \mathbb{R} \to S^1$, $p(x) = (\cos 2\pi x, \sin 2\pi x)$. It wraps the line round the circle like a spiral staircase seen from above, and every integer lands on $b_0 = (1, 0)$. Any open arc $U$ other than the whole circle is evenly covered: $p^{-1}(U)$ consists of disjoint open intervals, integer translates of each other, each mapped homeomorphically onto $U$.

Walk along a loop in the circle while a companion follows in the staircase, starting at $0$ and staying on the sheet they are on. When the loop closes, the companion is above $b_0$ again, at some integer $n$: the net number of anticlockwise turns. For example $\omega_n(s) = (\cos 2\pi n s, \sin 2\pi n s)$ lifts to $s \mapsto ns$ and ends at $n$.

blocks.title: Lifting lemma
blocks.body:
Let $p : E \to B$ be a covering map and $p(e_0) = b_0$.

1. Every path $f$ in $B$ starting at $b_0$ has a unique lift $\tilde f$, a path in $E$ with $p \circ \tilde f = f$ and $\tilde f(0) = e_0$.

2. Every path homotopy $F : [0,1]^2 \to B$ with $F(0,0) = b_0$ has a unique lift $\tilde F$ with $p \circ \tilde F = F$ and $\tilde F(0,0) = e_0$, and $\tilde F$ is again a path homotopy.

Consequently, if $f \simeq g$ are paths from $b_0$, then their lifts from $e_0$ end at the same point of $E$.

blocks.title: Proof sketch of the lifting lemma
blocks.body: Because $[0,1]$ is compact, the Lebesgue number lemma gives $0 = s_0 < s_1 < \dots < s_k = 1$ with each $f([s_{i-1}, s_i])$ inside an evenly covered set $U_i$. Lift piece by piece: $\tilde f(s_{i-1})$ lies in exactly one sheet $V$ over $U_i$, and on $[s_{i-1}, s_i]$ put $\tilde f = (p|_V)^{-1} \circ f$. Two lifts with the same start agree on a set that is open and closed in $[0,1]$, hence everywhere. A grid of small squares lifts homotopies in the same way. The edges $s = 0$ and $s = 1$ of the square map to single points, so their lifts are connected subsets of a discrete fibre $p^{-1}(b)$, hence single points: the lift is again a path homotopy.

blocks.title: The fundamental group of the circle
blocks.body: The map $\Phi : \mathbb{Z} \to \pi_1(S^1, b_0)$, $\Phi(n) = [\omega_n]$ with $\omega_n(s) = (\cos 2\pi n s, \sin 2\pi n s)$, is an isomorphism of groups. In particular $\pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Use $p : \mathbb{R} \to S^1$ with $e_0 = 0$. For a loop $f$ at $b_0$ let $\tilde f$ be its lift from $0$. Since $p(\tilde f(1)) = b_0$, the end point $\tilde f(1)$ is an integer, the degree of $f$. By the lifting lemma, path-homotopic loops have the same degree, so degree is a well-defined function on $\pi_1(S^1, b_0)$.

Surjective. If $f$ has degree $n$, the paths $\tilde f$ and $s \mapsto ns$ both run from $0$ to $n$ in $\mathbb{R}$, so $G(s,t) = (1-t)\tilde f(s) + t\,ns$ is a path homotopy between them, and $p \circ G$ is a path homotopy from $f$ to $\omega_n$. So $[f] = \Phi(n)$.

Injective. $\omega_n$ has degree $n$, so $\omega_m \simeq \omega_n$ forces $m = n$.

Homomorphism. The lift of $\omega_m \cdot \omega_n$ from $0$ runs from $0$ to $m$ along $2ms$ and then from $m$ to $m+n$ along $m + n(2s - 1)$; it is a lift because $p$ is unchanged by integer translations. So $\omega_m \cdot \omega_n$ has degree $m+n$ and, by surjectivity, is homotopic to $\omega_{m+n}$: $\Phi(m)\Phi(n) = \Phi(m+n)$.

blocks.title: Punctured plane and torus
blocks.body: Compute the fundamental groups of $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$ and of the torus $T = S^1 \times S^1$, and show that no two of $\mathbb{R}^2$, $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$ and $T$ are homeomorphic.
blocks.solution:
Let $r(x) = x / |x|$ map $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$ to $S^1$, and let $i$ be the inclusion of $S^1$, so $r \circ i = \mathrm{id}$. For a loop $f$ at $b_0 = (1,0)$, $H(s,t) = (1-t) f(s) + t\, f(s)/|f(s)|$ is a path homotopy from $f$ to $i \circ r \circ f$; it avoids $0$ because $f(s)$ and $f(s)/|f(s)|$ point the same way. Hence $r_* i_* = \mathrm{id}$ and $i_* r_* = \mathrm{id}$, and $\pi_1(\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.

For the torus the product rule gives $\pi_1(T) \cong \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$, generated by the classes $a$, $b$ of loops round the two circles, with $ab = ba$.

The groups $0$, $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ are pairwise non-isomorphic (quotienting by the subgroup of doubles leaves groups of orders $1$, $2$ and $4$), so no two of the spaces are homeomorphic.

blocks.title: No retraction, and Brouwer's fixed point theorem in the plane
blocks.body: Let $D$ be the closed unit disc. Show that there is no continuous $r : D \to S^1$ with $r(x) = x$ for all $x \in S^1$, and deduce that every continuous map $g : D \to D$ has a fixed point.
blocks.solution:
If such an $r$ exists and $i : S^1 \to D$ is the inclusion, then $r_* \circ i_*$ is the identity of $\pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. But $D$ is convex, so $\pi_1(D)$ is trivial and $r_* \circ i_*$ factors through the trivial group. Contradiction.

Now suppose $g : D \to D$ has no fixed point. Follow the ray from $g(x)$ through $x$ until it leaves the disc, at $r(x) = x + \lambda (x - g(x))$ with $\lambda \ge 0$. Here $\lambda$ is the larger root of the quadratic $|x + \lambda(x - g(x))|^2 = 1$, whose leading coefficient $|x - g(x)|^2$ never vanishes, so $r$ is continuous. For $x \in S^1$ the roots are $0$ and $-2(1 - x \cdot g(x))/|x - g(x)|^2 \le 0$, so $r(x) = x$. Thus $r$ is a retraction of $D$ onto $S^1$, which is impossible.

blocks.title: The fundamental theorem of algebra
blocks.body: Using winding numbers, show that a polynomial $q(z) = z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \dots + a_0$ with complex coefficients and $n \ge 1$ has a root in $\mathbb{C}$.
blocks.solution:
Suppose $q$ has no root, and fix $R_1 > \max(1, |a_0| + \dots + |a_{n-1}|)$. View $S^1$ as the unit complex numbers with $p(x) = e^{2\pi i x}$, and define the degree of any loop $\gamma$ in $S^1$ as $\tilde\gamma(1) - \tilde\gamma(0)$ for a lift $\tilde\gamma$; it is an integer, independent of the lift. Let $\gamma_R(s) = q(R e^{2\pi i s}) / |q(R e^{2\pi i s})|$ for $R \ge 0$. Lifting $(s, R) \mapsto \gamma_R(s)$ on $[0,1] \times [0, R_1]$ by the grid argument of the lifting lemma makes the degree of $\gamma_R$ a continuous integer-valued function of $R$, hence constant; at $R = 0$ the loop is constant, of degree $0$.

On $|z| = R_1$,
$$|a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \dots + a_0| \le (|a_{n-1}| + \dots + |a_0|) R_1^{n-1} < R_1^n = |z^n|,$$
so $q_t(z) = z^n + t(a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \dots + a_0)$ has no zero on that circle for $0 \le t \le 1$. The same continuity argument in $t$ shows that $\gamma_{R_1}$ has the degree of $s \mapsto e^{2\pi i n s}$, which is $n \ne 0$. Contradiction.

For $q(z) = z^3 - 2z + 5$, say, the image of $|z| = 8$ winds $3$ times round $0$ and that of $|z| = 1/2$ winds $0$ times, so the roots lie between these circles.

blocks.title: Beyond the circle: van Kampen and the classification of coverings
blocks.body:
Two theorems carry the subject further. They are stated here without proof.

Seifert–van Kampen. Let $X = U \cup V$ with $U$, $V$ open and path-connected, $U \cap V$ path-connected and $x_0 \in U \cap V$. Then $\pi_1(X, x_0)$ is the free product of $\pi_1(U, x_0)$ and $\pi_1(V, x_0)$ modulo the relations $i_1(w) = i_2(w)$, $w \in \pi_1(U \cap V, x_0)$, where $i_1, i_2$ come from the inclusions. For the figure eight (two circles joined at a point) it gives the free group on two generators $a, b$, in which $ab \ne ba$. For $S^k$ with $k \ge 2$, minus either pole, both pieces are contractible and their intersection is path-connected, so $S^k$ is simply connected. (So in dimension $n \ge 3$ the fundamental group cannot prove Brouwer's theorem, and [[homology]] is needed.) Gluing a disc along a loop kills its class, which gives the groups of the surfaces in [[classification-of-surfaces]].

Classification of coverings. For a covering $p : (\tilde X, \tilde x_0) \to (X, x_0)$, $p_*$ is injective (lift a homotopy that shrinks $p \circ \tilde f$). If $X$ is path-connected, locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected, its connected coverings correspond, up to isomorphism, to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $\pi_1(X)$, much as in [[galois]] theory. The trivial subgroup gives the simply connected universal cover, whose group of deck transformations (homeomorphisms commuting with $p$) is isomorphic to $\pi_1(X)$. For $S^1$ it is $\mathbb{R}$ with the integer translations, a free [[group-actions|group action]]; for the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$ (the sphere with antipodal points identified) it is $S^2$ with deck group $\{\pm\mathrm{id}\}$, so $\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^2) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$.

- Simply connected does not mean contractible: $S^2$ is simply connected, and its hole is detected by [[homology]].
- A surjective local homeomorphism need not be a covering: for $x \mapsto (\cos 2\pi x, \sin 2\pi x)$ on $(0, 2)$, no neighbourhood of $(1,0)$ is evenly covered.
- $\pi_1$ is not its abelianization: for the figure eight, $\pi_1$ is free on two generators, while $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}^2$.

The abelianization of $\pi_1(X)$ is the first [[homology]] group $H_1(X)$, and homology extends 'holes detected by loops' to every dimension. In complex analysis, the winding number behind the [[residues|residue theorem]] and [[continuation|analytic continuation]] along paths are statements about $\pi_1$ and coverings of punctured planes. The double cover $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ gives $\pi_1(SO(3)) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ (see [[lie-groups]]). The [[poincare|Poincaré conjecture]], proved by Perelman, says that a closed simply connected 3-manifold is homeomorphic to $S^3$.

1. Show that every continuous $g : S^1 \to \mathbb{R}$ takes equal values at some pair of antipodal points. (Hint: consider $g(x) - g(-x)$.)
2. Compute the fundamental groups of $S^1 \times \mathbb{R}^2$ and of the solid torus $S^1 \times D$.
3. Find a connected two-sheeted covering of the torus, and the subgroup of $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ it corresponds to.

Degree of omega_n computed by numerically lifting (accumulating small angle increments) equals n
For q(z)=z^3-2z+5: the bound sum |a_k| = 7, |lower terms| < |z^3| on |z|=8, the image of |z|=8 winds 3 times and the image of |z|=1/2 winds 0 times around 0

q=lambda z: z**3-2*z+5
def wind(R,N=200001):
    s=np.linspace(0,1,N); v=q(R*np.exp(2j*np.pi*s))
    assert np.min(np.abs(v))>0
    a=np.angle(v); d=np.diff(a); d=(d+np.pi)%(2*np.pi)-np.pi
    return d.sum()/(2*np.pi)
assert abs(-2)+abs(5)==7

entry.sum: Every closed surface (compact, connected, without boundary) is homeomorphic to exactly one of the sphere $S^2$, a connected sum of $g \ge 1$ tori, or a connected sum of $k \ge 1$ projective planes. Two closed surfaces are therefore homeomorphic exactly when they agree in orientability and in Euler characteristic $\chi = V - E + F$.
entry.why: It is the model of a complete classification theorem: an entire class of spaces is described by two numbers that can be read off from any triangulation. It is the starting point for the Gauss–Bonnet theorem, for the genus of Riemann surfaces and algebraic curves, and for drawing graphs on surfaces.

links.note: Euler's formula on a surface of characteristic $\chi$ bounds how dense an embedded graph can be, which gives Heawood's bound on the number of colours needed for maps on the torus and other surfaces.

Every compact Riemann surface is an orientable closed surface, so it is topologically determined by its genus $g$, which controls, through the Riemann–Hurwitz formula, how such surfaces can cover one another.
A smooth complex projective plane curve of degree $d$ is, as a real surface, a closed orientable surface of genus $(d-1)(d-2)/2$, so a smooth cubic curve is a torus.

blocks.body:
A sphere, the surface of a doughnut, the surface of a pretzel with three holes: all are two-dimensional, all are finite, none has an edge. How many essentially different such shapes are there, if we only care about shape up to stretching and bending (homeomorphism)? The answer, completed in the early twentieth century, is an explicit list, and you can place any surface on it by counting the vertices, edges and faces of a decomposition into polygons and checking whether it has two sides.

This page assumes [[topological-spaces]] (homeomorphisms, quotient spaces, compactness) and Euler's formula $V - E + F = 2$ for connected [[planar-graphs]].

blocks.title: Closed surface
blocks.body:
A surface is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space in which every point has an open neighbourhood homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$. A closed surface is a surface that is compact and connected. (Surfaces with boundary, such as the disc or the Möbius band, are allowed to have points with half-disc neighbourhoods; they are not closed surfaces.)

In words: a closed surface is a finite, edgeless, two-dimensional space that looks like a piece of the plane near every point.

blocks.title: Building surfaces from a polygon
blocks.body:
Take a polygon with an even number of sides and glue its sides in pairs. We record the gluing by a word: go round the boundary anticlockwise and write a letter for each side, with exponent $-1$ if the side's arrow points clockwise. Sides with the same letter are glued so that their arrows match.

1. $a a^{-1}$ (a two-sided polygon): zip the two sides together and you get the sphere $S^2$.
2. $a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$ (a square): gluing $a$ to $a^{-1}$ gives a cylinder, and then gluing its two end circles $b$ gives the torus $T^2$.
3. $a a$: a disc whose boundary circle is glued to itself by the antipodal map. This is the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$; it cannot be built inside $\mathbb{R}^3$ without self-intersection.
4. $a b a b^{-1}$: like the torus, but one pair is glued with a twist. This is the Klein bottle $K$.

Every polygon with paired sides gives a closed surface: points inside the polygon have disc neighbourhoods, points on glued sides get two half-discs that form a disc, and the corners that end up at one point fit together, one wedge from each corner, around that point.

A surface is orientable if it contains no Möbius band. For a polygon word this is easy to read off: the surface is orientable exactly when every letter appears once with exponent $+1$ and once with exponent $-1$. A pair $\dots x \dots x \dots$ with equal exponents gives a strip of the polygon whose ends are glued with a half-twist, which is a Möbius band.

blocks.title: Connected sum
blocks.body:
For closed surfaces $M$ and $N$, the connected sum $M \# N$ is obtained by removing a small open disc from each and gluing the two resulting boundary circles together. Up to homeomorphism it does not depend on which discs are removed. The sphere is a neutral element: $M \# S^2 \cong M$.

We write $T_g$ for the connected sum of $g$ tori (the surface of genus $g$, a pretzel with $g$ holes) and $N_k$ for the connected sum of $k$ projective planes. On the level of words, a connected sum is concatenation: $T_g$ is the $4g$-gon $a_1 b_1 a_1^{-1} b_1^{-1} \cdots a_g b_g a_g^{-1} b_g^{-1}$ and $N_k$ is the $2k$-gon $a_1 a_1 a_2 a_2 \cdots a_k a_k$. Each block $a b a^{-1} b^{-1}$ is called a handle and each block $a a$ a cross-cap. The Klein bottle is $N_2$.

blocks.title: Classification of closed surfaces
blocks.body:
Every closed surface is homeomorphic to exactly one of
$$S^2, \qquad T_g = \underbrace{T^2 \# \cdots \# T^2}_{g} \ (g \ge 1), \qquad N_k = \underbrace{\mathbb{RP}^2 \# \cdots \# \mathbb{RP}^2}_{k} \ (k \ge 1).$$
The surfaces $S^2$ and $T_g$ are orientable; the surfaces $N_k$ are not.

blocks.title: The Euler characteristic
blocks.body:
Cut a closed surface into polygons, with the edges forming a graph drawn on the surface, so that every face is an open disc. The number $\chi = V - E + F$ does not depend on how this is done; this is the Euler characteristic of the surface. (For the sphere this is Euler's formula. In general the invariance is proved with [[homology]], where $\chi$ is the alternating sum of the ranks of the homology groups.)

For a polygon model, $F = 1$, $E$ is half the number of sides, and $V$ is the number of classes of corners after gluing. In the word for $T_g$ all $4g$ corners become one point, so $\chi(T_g) = 1 - 2g + 1 = 2 - 2g$. In the word for $N_k$ all corners again become one point, so $\chi(N_k) = 1 - k + 1 = 2 - k$. And $\chi(S^2) = 2$.

For a connected sum: removing an open disc that is one face of a decomposition lowers $\chi$ by $1$, and gluing two boundary circles, each with the same number of vertices and edges, identifies equally many vertices and edges. So
$$\chi(M \# N) = \chi(M) + \chi(N) - 2.$$

Reading the list: orientable surfaces have $\chi = 2, 0, -2, -4, \dots$ and non-orientable ones have $\chi = 1, 0, -1, -2, \dots$. Each pair (orientability, $\chi$) occurs once, which gives the practical form of the theorem.

blocks.title: Classification by invariants
blocks.body: Two closed surfaces are homeomorphic if and only if they are both orientable or both non-orientable, and they have the same Euler characteristic.

blocks.title: Proof sketch of the classification
blocks.body:
Two inputs are taken from outside this page. Radó's theorem (1925): every surface can be triangulated. And invariance: orientability and $\chi$ do not depend on the triangulation, which can be proved with [[homology]]. Given these, the steps are as follows.

1. One polygon. A closed surface is compact, so a triangulation has finitely many triangles, and every edge lies in exactly two of them. Because the surface is connected, the triangles can be glued one at a time along an edge to a growing polygon, until one polygon remains whose sides are glued in pairs. So the surface is given by a word.

2. Cancel. A pair $x x^{-1}$ of adjacent sides folds shut like a book. Remove it, unless the whole word is $x x^{-1}$, which is the sphere.

3. One vertex. By cutting off a triangle at a corner of one vertex class and regluing it along the paired side, one can lower the number of corners in that class, and after repeating this (and cancelling) all corners are one point.

4. Cross-caps. If a letter appears twice with the same exponent, $\dots x \, P \, x \, Q$, cut along a diagonal and reglue along $x$; the new word contains an adjacent pair $y y$. Repeat until all such pairs are adjacent.

5. Handles. A remaining pair $x \dots x^{-1}$ must be interlinked with another pair $y \dots y^{-1}$ (otherwise the corners would fall into more than one class), and two more cut-and-paste moves gather them into a block $x y x^{-1} y^{-1}$.

6. Now the word is a product of handles and cross-caps. If it has at least one cross-cap, every handle can be turned into two cross-caps using the lemma $T^2 \# \mathbb{RP}^2 \cong N_3$, which is proved by one more cut-and-paste. So the word is $T_g$ or $N_k$.

Finally, the surfaces in the list are pairwise non-homeomorphic because their pairs (orientability, $\chi$) are different.

blocks.title: Reading off a word
blocks.body: Identify the closed surfaces given by the hexagon words $a b c a^{-1} b^{-1} c^{-1}$ and $a b a^{-1} b^{-1} c c$, and check that the second one is consistent with $T^2 \# \mathbb{RP}^2 \cong N_3$.
blocks.solution:
Label the corners $P_0, \dots, P_5$ anticlockwise, with side $i$ running from $P_i$ to $P_{i+1}$ (indices mod $6$).

First word, $a b c a^{-1} b^{-1} c^{-1}$. Side $0$ is $a$ from $P_0$ to $P_1$; side $3$ is $a^{-1}$, so as an arrow it runs from $P_4$ to $P_3$. Matching tails and heads glues $P_0 \sim P_4$ and $P_1 \sim P_3$. Similarly $b$ gives $P_1 \sim P_5$, $P_2 \sim P_4$, and $c$ gives $P_2 \sim P_0$, $P_3 \sim P_5$. The classes are $\{P_0, P_2, P_4\}$ and $\{P_1, P_3, P_5\}$, so $V = 2$, $E = 3$, $F = 1$ and $\chi = 0$. Each letter appears once with each exponent, so the surface is orientable. By the classification it is the torus. (One can see this directly: a regular hexagon with opposite sides glued by translation tiles the plane, just like a square.)

Second word, $a b a^{-1} b^{-1} c c$. The first four sides behave as for the torus and glue $P_0, \dots, P_4$ together; side $4$ is $c$ from $P_4$ to $P_5$ and side $5$ is $c$ from $P_5$ to $P_0$, so $P_4 \sim P_5$. All corners are one point: $V = 1$, $E = 3$, $F = 1$, $\chi = -1$. The letter $c$ appears twice with exponent $+1$, so the surface is non-orientable.

The word is the concatenation of a handle and a cross-cap, so the surface is $T^2 \# \mathbb{RP}^2$. Its invariants are those of $N_3$: $\chi(N_3) = 2 - 3 = -1$, also non-orientable. The connected-sum formula agrees: $\chi(T^2) + \chi(\mathbb{RP}^2) - 2 = 0 + 1 - 2 = -1$. So once a cross-cap is present, handles can be traded for pairs of cross-caps, and no separate family is needed.

blocks.title: How few triangles can a torus be cut into?
blocks.body: A triangulation of a closed surface is a decomposition into triangles in which any two triangles meet in a common edge, a common vertex, or not at all. In particular an edge is determined by its two end vertices. Show that a triangulation of the torus has at least $7$ vertices and a triangulation of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ at least $6$.
blocks.solution:
Each triangle has $3$ edges and each edge lies on exactly $2$ triangles, so $3F = 2E$. Hence
$$\chi = V - E + F = V - E + \tfrac23 E = V - \tfrac13 E, \qquad E = 3(V - \chi).$$
Since an edge is determined by its end points, $E \le \binom{V}{2} = \tfrac12 V(V-1)$. So
$$3(V - \chi) \le \tfrac12 V(V-1), \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad V^2 - 7V + 6\chi \ge 0.$$

For the torus, $\chi = 0$ gives $V(V - 7) \ge 0$, so $V \ge 7$. For $\mathbb{RP}^2$, $\chi = 1$ gives $(V-1)(V-6) \ge 0$; as $V > 1$, $V \ge 6$.

Both bounds are attained. With vertices $0, 1, \dots, 6$, take the $14$ triangles $\{i, i+1, i+3\}$ and $\{i, i+2, i+3\}$ for $i = 0, \dots, 6$, numbers mod $7$. Every one of the $\binom72 = 21$ pairs of vertices is an edge of exactly two triangles, and around each vertex its six triangles close up into a hexagon, so this is a closed surface with $\chi = 7 - 21 + 14 = 0$. Every edge is shared by two triangles that induce opposite orientations on it when the triangles are oriented as $(i, i+1, i+3)$ and $(i, i+3, i+2)$, so it is orientable: it is a torus. For $\mathbb{RP}^2$, the regular icosahedron is symmetric under $x \mapsto -x$; identifying opposite points gives $6$ vertices, $15$ edges and $10$ triangles, and $\chi = 1$.

The same inequality, applied to a graph drawn on the surface, is the starting point of Heawood's estimate for colouring maps on surfaces.

blocks.body:
- The Euler characteristic alone does not classify. The torus and the Klein bottle both have $\chi = 0$; orientability distinguishes them.
- The theorem is about closed surfaces. Surfaces with boundary are classified by orientability, $\chi$ and the number of boundary circles (the annulus and the Möbius band both have $\chi = 0$; the annulus is orientable with two boundary circles, the Möbius band is not and has one). Non-compact surfaces, like the plane minus a Cantor set, need much more data.
- Non-orientable closed surfaces exist perfectly well as abstract spaces, but none of them can be embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Pictures of the Klein bottle in space always have a self-intersection.
- Apply cut-and-paste steps to the word, not to a drawing, and re-check $\chi$ and orientability after each step.
- For words, 'number of vertices' means the number of classes of corners after gluing, not the number of corners of the polygon.

The fundamental group distinguishes the surfaces too: by the Seifert–van Kampen theorem, $\pi_1(T_g)$ has generators $a_1, b_1, \dots, a_g, b_g$ and one relation $\prod_i a_i b_i a_i^{-1} b_i^{-1} = 1$, which is just the polygon word (see [[fundamental-group]]). The first [[homology]] groups are $H_1(T_g) \cong \mathbb{Z}^{2g}$ and $H_1(N_k) \cong \mathbb{Z}^{k-1} \oplus \mathbb{Z}/2$. The Euler characteristic reappears in [[gauss-bonnet|the Gauss–Bonnet theorem]]: for any Riemannian metric on a closed orientable surface, the total Gaussian curvature equals $2\pi\chi$ (the formula also holds for non-orientable surfaces, with area measured as a density). Euler's formula for [[planar-graphs]] is the case of the sphere, and an inequality of the same kind as in the last example is how one proves that $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$ are not planar. In dimension three no list of this kind is possible in the same simple form; the [[poincare|Poincaré conjecture]] and Thurston's geometrization describe what replaces it.

1. Compute the Euler characteristic and orientability of the surface with word $a b c a b c$, and identify it.
2. Show that the Klein bottle can be cut into two Möbius bands, and deduce $\chi(\text{Möbius band}) = 0$ from $\chi(K) = 0$.
3. A cube has its six faces; glue each face to the opposite one by the map $x \mapsto -x$ (the cube centred at the origin). Is the result a closed surface? If so, which one?
4. Show that $N_{2g+1} \cong T_g \# \mathbb{RP}^2$ and $N_{2g+2} \cong T_g \# K$.

def snf_diag(M):
    # M: list of lists of ints; returns nonzero invariant factors via integer elimination
    A=[row[:] for row in M]; m=len(A); n=len(A[0]) if m else 0; diag=[]; r=0
    for c in range(n):
        if r>=m: break
        while True:
            piv=[(abs(A[i][j]),i,j) for i in range(r,m) for j in range(c,n) if A[i][j]!=0]
            if not piv: return diag
            _,pi,pj=min(piv)
            A[r],A[pi]=A[pi],A[r]
            for row in A: row[c],row[pj]=row[pj],row[c]
            done=True
            for i in range(r+1,m):
                q=A[i][c]//A[r][c]
                if q:
                    A[i]=[x-q*y for x,y in zip(A[i],A[r])]
                if A[i][c]!=0: done=False
            for j in range(c+1,n):
                q=A[r][j]//A[r][c]
                if q:
                    for i in range(m): A[i][j]-=q*A[i][c]
                if A[r][j]!=0: done=False
            if done:
                bad=[(i,j) for i in range(r+1,m) for j in range(c+1,n) if A[i][j]%A[r][c]]
                if bad:
                    i,_=bad[0]; A[r]=[x+y for x,y in zip(A[r],A[i])]; continue
                diag.append(abs(A[r][c])); r+=1; break
    return diag
def homology(dims, mats):
    # mats[k]: matrix of d_k : C_k -> C_{k-1} as rows=dim C_{k-1}, cols=dim C_k ; returns [(betti, torsion)]
    out=[]
    for k in range(len(dims)):
        rk_out=len(snf_diag(mats[k])) if k in mats and dims[k-1]>0 else 0
        inv=snf_diag(mats[k+1]) if (k+1) in mats else []
        out.append((dims[k]-rk_out-len(inv), sorted(d for d in inv if d>1)))
    return out
from itertools import combinations
def simplicial(maximal):
    S=set()
    for m in maximal:
        m=tuple(sorted(m))
        for k in range(1,len(m)+1):
            S.update(combinations(m,k))
    top=max(len(s) for s in S)-1
    faces=[sorted(s for s in S if len(s)==k+1) for k in range(top+1)]
    mats={}
    for k in range(1,top+1):
        idx={f:i for i,f in enumerate(faces[k-1])}
        M=[[0]*len(faces[k]) for _ in faces[k-1]]
        for j,s in enumerate(faces[k]):
            for i in range(len(s)): M[idx[s[:i]+s[i+1:]]][j]+=(-1)**i
        mats[k]=M
    return [len(f) for f in faces], mats, faces

entry.sum: Homology assigns to a space $X$ a sequence of abelian groups $H_0(X), H_1(X), H_2(X), \dots$, where $H_n(X)$ measures the $n$-dimensional holes: $n$-dimensional cycles (chains with zero boundary) modulo those that are themselves boundaries. It is built from the single algebraic fact $\partial \circ \partial = 0$, it is unchanged by homotopy equivalence, and, unlike the fundamental group, it sees holes of every dimension and can be computed by linear algebra over $\mathbb{Z}$.
entry.why: Homology proves that $\mathbb{R}^m \not\cong \mathbb{R}^n$ for $m \ne n$, gives Brouwer's fixed point theorem in every dimension, and explains why the Euler characteristic is an invariant. Its algebra (chain complexes and exact sequences) has become a standard tool in algebra, geometry and data analysis.

links.note: De Rham's theorem identifies the cohomology built from closed and exact differential forms on a smooth manifold with singular cohomology with real coefficients, so integrals of forms over cycles detect topology.

Persistent homology, used in topological data analysis, computes the homology of a growing family of simplicial complexes built from a point cloud and records which holes appear and disappear as the scale changes.

refs: Massey, A Basic Course in Algebraic Topology

blocks.body:
The [[fundamental-group]] detects holes that a loop can wind around. It is blind to the hole inside a hollow sphere: every loop on $S^2$ can be shrunk to a point. Yet the hollow sphere obviously encloses something that the solid ball does not. Homology captures this by asking a different question: not whether a loop can be shrunk, but whether a closed curve, closed surface or closed higher-dimensional piece is the boundary of something inside the space.

The answer is a sequence of abelian groups, one for each dimension. In dimension one they are coarser than the fundamental group, but they are much easier to compute and they work in every dimension. This page assumes the [[fundamental-group]] and [[group-homomorphisms|quotient groups]]; some familiarity with [[modules]] over $\mathbb{Z}$ (finitely generated abelian groups) helps.

blocks.title: Cycles that bound and cycles that do not
blocks.body:
Take a triangle with vertices $0, 1, 2$, and first consider only its three edges (a hollow triangle, which is a circle). Orient each edge from the smaller to the larger vertex and define the boundary of an edge as end minus start: $\partial[0,1] = [1] - [0]$, and so on. Formal integer combinations of edges are called $1$-chains. The chain
$$z = [0,1] + [1,2] - [0,2]$$
goes once round the triangle, and its boundary is $([1]-[0]) + ([2]-[1]) - ([2]-[0]) = 0$. A chain with zero boundary is a cycle.

Now fill in the triangle by adding a $2$-dimensional piece $[0,1,2]$, with boundary
$$\partial[0,1,2] = [1,2] - [0,2] + [0,1] = z.$$
In the filled triangle the cycle $z$ is the boundary of something, while in the hollow triangle it is not. Homology in dimension one is exactly 'cycles modulo boundaries': it is $\mathbb{Z}$ (generated by $z$) for the hollow triangle and $0$ for the filled one. The same idea in one dimension higher distinguishes the hollow tetrahedron (a sphere) from the solid one.

blocks.title: Simplicial chain complex
blocks.body:
Let $K$ be a finite simplicial complex whose vertices are numbered. An $n$-simplex is written $[v_0, \dots, v_n]$ with $v_0 < \dots < v_n$. The chain group $C_n(K)$ is the free abelian group with basis the $n$-simplices of $K$. The boundary map $\partial_n : C_n(K) \to C_{n-1}(K)$ is the homomorphism defined on basis elements by
$$\partial_n [v_0, \dots, v_n] = \sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i \, [v_0, \dots, \widehat{v_i}, \dots, v_n],$$
where the hat means that $v_i$ is left out; $\partial_0 = 0$. Elements of $Z_n = \ker \partial_n$ are $n$-cycles and elements of $B_n = \operatorname{im} \partial_{n+1}$ are $n$-boundaries.

In words: the boundary of a simplex is the alternating sum of its faces, with the signs keeping track of orientation.

blocks.title: The boundary of a boundary is zero
blocks.body: For every $n \ge 1$, $\partial_{n-1} \circ \partial_n = 0$. Consequently $B_n \subseteq Z_n$.

It suffices to check a basis element $\sigma = [v_0, \dots, v_n]$. Applying $\partial$ twice removes two vertices $v_j$ and $v_i$ with $j < i$, and each such face arises in two ways. Removing $v_i$ first contributes the sign $(-1)^i$, and then $v_j$ is still in position $j$, contributing $(-1)^j$. Removing $v_j$ first contributes $(-1)^j$, and then $v_i$ has moved to position $i - 1$, contributing $(-1)^{i-1}$. The two terms are $(-1)^{i+j}$ and $-(-1)^{i+j}$ times the same simplex, so they cancel, and $\partial\partial\sigma = 0$.

blocks.title: Homology group
blocks.body:
The $n$-th homology group of $K$ is the quotient
$$H_n(K) = Z_n / B_n = \ker \partial_n / \operatorname{im} \partial_{n+1}.$$
It is a finitely generated abelian group, so $H_n(K) \cong \mathbb{Z}^{\beta_n} \oplus T_n$ with $T_n$ finite. The number $\beta_n$ is the $n$-th Betti number and $T_n$ is the torsion.

In words: $n$-dimensional cycles, where two cycles count as the same if they differ by a boundary.

blocks.title: Circle, disc and sphere by linear algebra
blocks.body: Compute the homology of the hollow triangle, the filled triangle, and the boundary of a tetrahedron (four triangles on vertices $0, 1, 2, 3$).
blocks.solution:
Hollow triangle. $C_0 = \mathbb{Z}^3$, $C_1 = \mathbb{Z}^3$. With edges ordered $[0,1], [0,2], [1,2]$, the matrix of $\partial_1$ has columns $(-1, 1, 0)$, $(-1, 0, 1)$, $(0, -1, 1)$. Its rank is $2$, so $\ker \partial_1 \cong \mathbb{Z}$, generated by $z = [0,1] + [1,2] - [0,2]$, and $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}$. In degree $0$ every vertex is a cycle, and the boundaries $[j] - [i]$ make all vertices equal, so $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}^3 / B_0 \cong \mathbb{Z}$.

Filled triangle. Now $\partial_2 [0,1,2] = z$, so $B_1 = Z_1$ and $H_1 = 0$. The map $\partial_2$ is injective, so $H_2 = 0$. As for a point, only $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$ survives.

Boundary of a tetrahedron. There are $4$ vertices, $6$ edges and $4$ triangles. The rank of $\partial_1$ is $3$ (the graph is connected, and a connected graph on $4$ vertices has boundary map of rank $4 - 1$), so $\ker\partial_1$ has rank $6 - 3 = 3$. The images of the four triangles satisfy exactly one relation,
$$\partial([1,2,3] - [0,2,3] + [0,1,3] - [0,1,2]) = 0,$$
so $\partial_2$ has rank $3$ and kernel $\mathbb{Z}$, spanned by the alternating sum above: that cycle is the whole sphere, oriented. One checks that $B_1 = Z_1$ (each of the three independent triangle-cycles is a boundary). So $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1 = 0$, $H_2 = \mathbb{Z}$. The hollow sphere has a $2$-dimensional hole and no $1$-dimensional one, which is what the fundamental group could not say.

blocks.title: Singular homology and its main properties
blocks.body:
Simplicial homology depends, on the face of it, on a chosen triangulation. Singular homology removes the choice: $C_n(X)$ is the free abelian group on all continuous maps $\sigma : \Delta^n \to X$ from the standard $n$-simplex, with the same alternating boundary formula applied to the faces of $\Delta^n$. The proof that $\partial\partial = 0$ is the computation above. The resulting groups $H_n(X)$ are defined for every space, and for a simplicial complex they agree with the simplicial ones; this and the following facts are standard theorems, stated here without proof.

1. Functoriality. A continuous map $f : X \to Y$ induces homomorphisms $f_* : H_n(X) \to H_n(Y)$, with $(g f)_* = g_* f_*$ and $\mathrm{id}_* = \mathrm{id}$.
2. Homotopy invariance. Homotopic maps induce the same homomorphisms. Hence homotopy equivalent spaces have isomorphic homology; for example any convex set, or $\mathbb{R}^n$, has the homology of a point: $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$ and $H_n = 0$ for $n \ge 1$.
3. Degree zero. $H_0(X)$ is free abelian on the path components of $X$.
4. Degree one (Hurewicz). For path-connected $X$, $H_1(X)$ is the abelianization of $\pi_1(X)$.
5. Mayer–Vietoris. If $X$ is the union of the interiors of subspaces $A$ and $B$, there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots \to H_n(A \cap B) \to H_n(A) \oplus H_n(B) \to H_n(X) \to H_{n-1}(A \cap B) \to \cdots$$
Exact means that at each place the image of the incoming map equals the kernel of the outgoing one.

It is often convenient to use reduced homology $\tilde H_n$, which is the same as $H_n$ except that $\tilde H_0(X) \oplus \mathbb{Z} \cong H_0(X)$ for non-empty $X$. A point has $\tilde H_n = 0$ in every degree, and Mayer–Vietoris holds for reduced homology when $A \cap B$ is non-empty.

blocks.title: Homology of spheres
blocks.body: For $k \ge 0$, $\tilde H_n(S^k) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ if $n = k$ and $\tilde H_n(S^k) = 0$ otherwise.

Induction on $k$. The sphere $S^0$ is two points, so $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}^2$, $\tilde H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$ and all other groups vanish. For $k \ge 1$, let $A$ and $B$ be the sphere minus the south pole and minus the north pole. Both are homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^k$, so their reduced homology is zero, and $A \cap B$ is homotopy equivalent to the equator $S^{k-1}$. In the reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence
$$\tilde H_n(A) \oplus \tilde H_n(B) \to \tilde H_n(S^k) \to \tilde H_{n-1}(A \cap B) \to \tilde H_{n-1}(A) \oplus \tilde H_{n-1}(B)$$
the outer groups are $0$, so exactness gives $\tilde H_n(S^k) \cong \tilde H_{n-1}(S^{k-1})$ for every $n$. The induction hypothesis finishes the proof.

blocks.title: Brouwer's theorem and invariance of dimension
blocks.body: Using the homology of spheres, show (a) that every continuous map $g : D^n \to D^n$ of the closed $n$-ball has a fixed point, and (b) that $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ are not homeomorphic when $m \ne n$.
blocks.solution:
(a) As in the two-dimensional case on the [[fundamental-group]] page, a fixed-point-free $g$ would give a retraction $r : D^n \to S^{n-1}$ (send $x$ to the point where the ray from $g(x)$ through $x$ leaves the ball), so $r \circ i = \mathrm{id}$ for the inclusion $i : S^{n-1} \to D^n$. Apply $\tilde H_{n-1}$: the identity of $\tilde H_{n-1}(S^{n-1}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ would factor through $\tilde H_{n-1}(D^n) = 0$, because the ball is convex. That is impossible, so $g$ has a fixed point. For $n = 1$ this is the intermediate value theorem, and the argument uses $\tilde H_0(S^0) = \mathbb{Z}$.

(b) Suppose $h : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a homeomorphism, and $m, n \ge 1$. Removing a point and its image, $h$ restricts to a homeomorphism $\mathbb{R}^m \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{h(0)\}$. The space $\mathbb{R}^m \setminus \{0\}$ deformation retracts onto $S^{m-1}$ by $x \mapsto x/|x|$, so its reduced homology is $\mathbb{Z}$ in degree $m - 1$ and $0$ elsewhere; similarly for $n$. Isomorphic homology forces $m - 1 = n - 1$. (If one of them is $0$, $\mathbb{R}^0$ is a point and cannot be homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n \ge 1$.)

The fundamental group of the punctured space only separates $\mathbb{R}^2$ from the other $\mathbb{R}^n$, since $S^k$ is simply connected for $k \ge 2$; homology separates all of them.

blocks.title: Torus and Klein bottle: torsion appears
blocks.body:
Take a square with corners $bl, br, tr, tl$ (bottom left, and so on). The two horizontal sides are both called $a$ and run left to right. For the torus the vertical sides are both $b$, running upwards, and the diagonal $c$ runs from $bl$ to $tr$, cutting the square into the triangles $U = [bl, br, tr]$ and $L = [bl, tl, tr]$. For the Klein bottle the left side $b$ runs upwards but the right side $b$ runs downwards, and the diagonal $c$ runs from $tl$ to $br$, giving $U = [tl, tr, br]$ and $L = [bl, tl, br]$. In both cases the four corners become one vertex $v$, and the boundary formula $\partial[p,q,r] = [q,r] - [p,r] + [p,q]$ gives
$$\text{torus: } \partial U = a + b - c, \quad \partial L = a + b - c; \qquad \text{Klein bottle: } \partial U = a + b - c, \quad \partial L = -a + b + c.$$
Compute $H_0, H_1, H_2$ in both cases. (This uses $\Delta$-complexes, where faces of one simplex may be glued together; the chain complex is defined by the same formula.)
blocks.solution:
Every edge starts and ends at $v$, so $\partial_1 = 0$ and $Z_1 = C_1 = \mathbb{Z}^3$. Also $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$.

Torus. The image of $\partial_2$ is generated by $x = a + b - c$. Since $\{a, b, x\}$ is again a basis of $\mathbb{Z}^3$ (because $c = a + b - x$), $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}^3 / \langle x \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$, generated by $a$ and $b$. The kernel of $\partial_2$ is spanned by $U - L$, so $H_2 = \mathbb{Z}$. This matches the Hurewicz statement: $\pi_1(T^2) = \mathbb{Z}^2$ is already abelian.

Klein bottle. Now $\operatorname{im}\partial_2$ is generated by $x = a + b - c$ and $-a + b + c = 2b - x$, so it is $\langle x, 2b \rangle$. In the basis $\{x, b, c\}$ of $\mathbb{Z}^3$ this subgroup is $\mathbb{Z} x \oplus 2\mathbb{Z} b$, so
$$H_1(K) \cong \mathbb{Z}^3 / (\mathbb{Z} x \oplus 2\mathbb{Z} b) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2 \oplus \mathbb{Z}.$$
If $m U + n L$ is a cycle, then $m(a + b - c) + n(-a + b + c) = 0$ gives $m = n$ and $m + n = 0$, so $m = n = 0$: $H_2(K) = 0$.

Two lessons. First, homology can have torsion: the class $b$ is not a boundary, but $2b$ is. Second, $H_2 = \mathbb{Z}$ for the torus and $0$ for the Klein bottle reflects orientability: by a standard theorem (not proved here), a closed connected $n$-manifold has $H_n \cong \mathbb{Z}$ if it is orientable and $H_n = 0$ if not. In both cases $\chi = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0 = \beta_0 - \beta_1 + \beta_2$.

blocks.title: Euler characteristic
blocks.body:
For a finite simplicial (or $\Delta$-) complex $K$ with $c_n$ simplices of dimension $n$,
$$\sum_n (-1)^n c_n = \sum_n (-1)^n \beta_n.$$
In particular the left side does not depend on the triangulation, since the right side is a homotopy invariant.

Tensor with $\mathbb{Q}$, or simply take ranks of the free abelian groups involved. Let $z_n = \operatorname{rank} Z_n$ and $b_n = \operatorname{rank} B_n$. Rank–nullity for $\partial_n : C_n \to C_{n-1}$ gives $c_n = z_n + b_{n-1}$, and the definition of $H_n$ gives $\beta_n = z_n - b_n$, since torsion does not contribute to rank. Then
$$\sum_n (-1)^n c_n = \sum_n (-1)^n z_n + \sum_n (-1)^n b_{n-1} = \sum_n (-1)^n z_n - \sum_n (-1)^n b_n = \sum_n (-1)^n \beta_n,$$
where the middle step shifts the index in the second sum.

- Homology is coarser than homotopy type. The Poincaré homology sphere has the same homology as $S^3$ but a non-trivial fundamental group (of order $120$), and $H_1$ only remembers $\pi_1$ up to abelianization.
- Betti numbers forget torsion. Over $\mathbb{Q}$ the Klein bottle and the circle have the same homology; with integer coefficients, $H_1(K) = \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}/2$ tells them apart.
- Signs matter. Dropping the signs in the boundary formula breaks $\partial\partial = 0$ (unless one works mod $2$, which is a legitimate but different theory with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}/2$).
- $H_0$ of a non-empty space is never $0$; it is the reduced group $\tilde H_0$ that vanishes for connected spaces.
- A cycle need not be an embedded loop or sphere: twice a loop, or a sum of loops in different places, is also a cycle.

The Euler characteristic in [[classification-of-surfaces]] is the alternating sum of Betti numbers, and $H_1(T_g) = \mathbb{Z}^{2g}$, $H_1(N_k) = \mathbb{Z}^{k-1} \oplus \mathbb{Z}/2$ give an independent proof that the surfaces in that list are distinct. Dualising gives cohomology, which carries a product; on smooth manifolds de Rham's theorem computes it with [[differential-forms]], and the [[gauss-bonnet|Gauss–Bonnet theorem]] expresses $\chi$ as an integral of curvature. The structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain (see [[modules]]) is exactly what makes $H_n$ computable via the Smith normal form of the boundary matrices. The Lefschetz fixed point theorem and Poincaré duality start from this machinery, and the [[hodge|Hodge conjecture]] asks which rational cohomology classes of smooth complex projective varieties come from subvarieties.

1. Compute the simplicial homology of the complex consisting of two triangles $[0,1,2]$ and $[0,2,3]$ together with the extra edge $[1,3]$.
2. Use Mayer–Vietoris to compute the homology of the wedge of two circles and of the torus minus a point.
3. Show that the antipodal map of $S^n$ is not homotopic to the identity when $n$ is even, given that it acts on $\tilde H_n(S^n)$ as multiplication by $(-1)^{n+1}$.
4. The real projective plane is a $\Delta$-complex with two vertices, three edges and two triangles; with suitable orientations $\partial U = -a + b + c$, $\partial L = a - b + c$ and $\partial a = \partial b = w - v$, $\partial c = 0$. Compute its homology.

def snf_diag(M):
    # M: list of lists of ints; returns nonzero invariant factors via integer elimination
    A=[row[:] for row in M]; m=len(A); n=len(A[0]) if m else 0; diag=[]; r=0
    for c in range(n):
        if r>=m: break
        while True:
            piv=[(abs(A[i][j]),i,j) for i in range(r,m) for j in range(c,n) if A[i][j]!=0]
            if not piv: return diag
            _,pi,pj=min(piv)
            A[r],A[pi]=A[pi],A[r]
            for row in A: row[c],row[pj]=row[pj],row[c]
            done=True
            for i in range(r+1,m):
                q=A[i][c]//A[r][c]
                if q:
                    A[i]=[x-q*y for x,y in zip(A[i],A[r])]
                if A[i][c]!=0: done=False
            for j in range(c+1,n):
                q=A[r][j]//A[r][c]
                if q:
                    for i in range(m): A[i][j]-=q*A[i][c]
                if A[r][j]!=0: done=False
            if done:
                bad=[(i,j) for i in range(r+1,m) for j in range(c+1,n) if A[i][j]%A[r][c]]
                if bad:
                    i,_=bad[0]; A[r]=[x+y for x,y in zip(A[r],A[i])]; continue
                diag.append(abs(A[r][c])); r+=1; break
    return diag
def homology(dims, mats):
    # mats[k]: matrix of d_k : C_k -> C_{k-1} as rows=dim C_{k-1}, cols=dim C_k ; returns [(betti, torsion)]
    out=[]
    for k in range(len(dims)):
        rk_out=len(snf_diag(mats[k])) if k in mats and dims[k-1]>0 else 0
        inv=snf_diag(mats[k+1]) if (k+1) in mats else []
        out.append((dims[k]-rk_out-len(inv), sorted(d for d in inv if d>1)))
    return out
from itertools import combinations
def simplicial(maximal):
    S=set()
    for m in maximal:
        m=tuple(sorted(m))
        for k in range(1,len(m)+1):
            S.update(combinations(m,k))
    top=max(len(s) for s in S)-1
    faces=[sorted(s for s in S if len(s)==k+1) for k in range(top+1)]
    mats={}
    for k in range(1,top+1):
        idx={f:i for i,f in enumerate(faces[k-1])}
        M=[[0]*len(faces[k]) for _ in faces[k-1]]
        for j,s in enumerate(faces[k]):
            for i in range(len(s)): M[idx[s[:i]+s[i+1:]]][j]+=(-1)**i
        mats[k]=M
    return [len(f) for f in faces], mats, faces

entry.sum: A regular curve $\alpha(t)$ in space can be reparametrised by arc length $s$, and then its unit tangent $T = \alpha'(s)$ turns at the rate $\kappa = |T'(s)|$, the curvature. For a space curve the Frenet frame $(T, N, B)$ moves according to the Frenet–Serret equations, and curvature and torsion together determine the curve up to a rigid motion.
key: T' = \kappa N, \qquad N' = -\kappa T + \tau B, \qquad B' = -\tau N \qquad (' = d/ds)
entry.why: Curvature is what a driver feels as sideways acceleration $\kappa v^2$ and what a road or railway designer controls when joining straight track to a bend. The Frenet frame is the prototype of a moving frame, the method later used for surfaces and for curvature in higher dimensions.

links.note: For a particle moving along a path, the acceleration splits into a tangential part $dv/dt$ and a normal part $\kappa v^2$ toward the centre of the osculating circle, which is the centripetal acceleration $v^2/r$ of circular motion with $r = 1/\kappa$.

The Frenet–Serret equations are a linear system of ordinary differential equations for the frame, and existence and uniqueness for such systems is exactly what proves that curvature and torsion determine a curve up to rigid motion.

refs: do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces

blocks.body:
Drive along a winding road at a steady speed. Your speed does not change, yet you feel pushed sideways in every bend, more in tight bends than in gentle ones. The quantity you feel is the rate at which your direction of travel turns, and that is what curvature measures. In space there is a second effect: a corkscrew path also twists out of any plane it momentarily lies in, and torsion measures that.

This page assumes [[parametric-polar|parametric curves]], [[vectors-plane|vectors]] including the dot and cross products, and [[derivative|derivatives]], which we take componentwise for vector functions.

blocks.title: Velocity, speed and arc length
blocks.body:
A parametrised curve is a smooth map $\alpha : I \to \mathbb{R}^3$ (or $\mathbb{R}^2$) from an interval. Its velocity is $\alpha'(t)$, its speed is $v(t) = |\alpha'(t)|$, and its acceleration is $\alpha''(t)$. The curve is regular if $\alpha'(t) \ne 0$ for all $t$: then it has a well-defined direction at every point, and we can speak of the unit tangent $T = \alpha'/|\alpha'|$.

The distance travelled from time $t_0$ to time $t$ is the arc length
$$s(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} |\alpha'(u)| \, du.$$
For example, the helix $\alpha(t) = (a\cos t, a\sin t, bt)$ with $a > 0$ has $\alpha'(t) = (-a\sin t, a\cos t, b)$ and constant speed $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$; one full turn has length $2\pi\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$; unrolling the cylinder, the turn becomes the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $2\pi a$ and $2\pi b$.

For a regular curve, $s'(t) = v(t) > 0$, so $s$ is strictly increasing and can be inverted; writing the curve as a function of $s$ gives a reparametrisation with $|d\alpha/ds| = 1$. Such unit-speed (arc-length) parametrisations are the natural ones for geometry, because quantities computed with them depend only on the shape of the curve, not on how fast it is traced. For the helix, $s = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\, t$, so $\beta(s) = \alpha(s / \sqrt{a^2 + b^2})$ is the unit-speed version.

blocks.title: Curvature
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha(s)$ be a unit-speed curve, so that $T(s) = \alpha'(s)$ is a unit vector. The curvature is $\kappa(s) = |T'(s)| = |\alpha''(s)|$. Where $\kappa > 0$, the principal normal is $N = T'/\kappa$, and the circle of radius $1/\kappa$ through $\alpha(s)$ with centre $\alpha(s) + N/\kappa$, lying in the plane of $T$ and $N$, is the osculating circle.

In words: curvature is how fast the direction turns per unit distance travelled, and $1/\kappa$ is the radius of the circle that fits the curve best at that point.

blocks.title: Computing curvature in any parametrisation
blocks.body:
Two facts about a unit vector field $T(s)$: differentiating $T \cdot T = 1$ gives $2\, T \cdot T' = 0$, so $T'$ is perpendicular to $T$; and on a circle of radius $r$ traced at unit speed, $\alpha(s) = (r\cos(s/r), r\sin(s/r), 0)$, we get $\alpha''(s) = -\frac1r(\cos(s/r), \sin(s/r), 0)$, so $\kappa = 1/r$ and $N$ points to the centre. A tight circle has large curvature; a straight line has $\kappa = 0$.

In practice curves rarely come with unit speed. For any regular parametrisation, write $\alpha' = v\, T$. By the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dt} T = v \frac{dT}{ds} = \kappa v N$, so
$$\alpha'' = v' \, T + \kappa v^2 N.$$
This is the decomposition of acceleration into a tangential part (change of speed) and a normal part (change of direction), the familiar $v^2/r$ of circular motion. Taking the cross product with $\alpha' = vT$ kills the first term:
$$\alpha' \times \alpha'' = \kappa v^3 \, (T \times N), \qquad\text{so}\qquad \kappa = \frac{|\alpha' \times \alpha''|}{|\alpha'|^3}.$$
For a plane curve $(x(t), y(t))$ this becomes $\kappa = |x'y'' - y'x''| / (x'^2 + y'^2)^{3/2}$, and for a graph $y = f(x)$ it is $\kappa = |f''| / (1 + f'^2)^{3/2}$. Without the absolute value, $k = (x'y'' - y'x'')/(x'^2+y'^2)^{3/2}$ is the signed curvature of a plane curve, positive when the curve turns to the left.

blocks.title: Parabola, ellipse and a cycloid
blocks.body: (a) Find the curvature of the parabola $y = x^2$ and where it is largest. (b) Find the curvature of the ellipse $(a \cos t, b \sin t)$ with $a > b > 0$ at the ends of its axes. (c) Find the length of one arch of the cycloid $(t - \sin t, 1 - \cos t)$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, traced by a point on a rolling wheel of radius $1$.
blocks.solution:
(a) With $f(x) = x^2$, $\kappa(x) = 2 / (1 + 4x^2)^{3/2}$. This is largest at $x = 0$, where $\kappa = 2$: the osculating circle at the vertex has radius $\tfrac12$ and centre $(0, \tfrac12)$. Far out, $\kappa \to 0$ and the parabola looks almost straight.

(b) Here $x' = -a\sin t$, $y' = b\cos t$, $x'' = -a\cos t$, $y'' = -b \sin t$, so $x'y'' - y'x'' = ab\sin^2 t + ab\cos^2 t = ab$ and
$$\kappa(t) = \frac{ab}{(a^2 \sin^2 t + b^2 \cos^2 t)^{3/2}}.$$
At $t = 0$ (the end of the long axis) $\kappa = ab/b^3 = a/b^2$; at $t = \pi/2$ (the end of the short axis) $\kappa = b/a^2$. For $a = 2$, $b = 1$: $\kappa = 2$ at the sharp ends and $\tfrac14$ at the flat sides.

(c) The velocity is $(1 - \cos t, \sin t)$, so $v^2 = 2 - 2\cos t = 4\sin^2(t/2)$ and $v = 2\sin(t/2)$ for $0 \le t \le 2\pi$. The length is
$$\int_0^{2\pi} 2 \sin(t/2)\, dt = \Big[-4\cos(t/2)\Big]_0^{2\pi} = 8,$$
four times the diameter of the wheel. Note that $v = 0$ at $t = 0$ and $t = 2\pi$: the cycloid is not regular there, and it has cusps.

blocks.title: Torsion and the Frenet frame
blocks.body: For a unit-speed space curve with $\kappa > 0$, the vectors $T$ and $N$ are perpendicular unit vectors. Complete them to a right-handed orthonormal frame with the binormal $B = T \times N$. This Frenet frame travels along the curve. The plane spanned by $T$ and $N$, the osculating plane, is the plane the curve 'almost lies in' near the point; $B$ is its normal. If the curve lies in a plane, $B$ is constant. In general $B$ turns, and the rate at which it turns, measured with a sign, is the torsion.

blocks.title: Frenet–Serret equations
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha(s)$ be a unit-speed curve in $\mathbb{R}^3$, three times differentiable, with $\kappa(s) > 0$. There is a function $\tau(s)$, the torsion, such that
$$T' = \kappa N, \qquad N' = -\kappa T + \tau B, \qquad B' = -\tau N.$$
For an arbitrary regular parametrisation, $\tau = (\alpha' \times \alpha'') \cdot \alpha''' / |\alpha' \times \alpha''|^2$.

The first equation is the definition of $N$. For the third, differentiate $B = T \times N$:
$$B' = T' \times N + T \times N' = \kappa N \times N + T \times N' = T \times N'.$$
So $B'$ is perpendicular to $T$. It is also perpendicular to $B$, because $B$ is a unit vector. Hence $B'$ is a multiple of $N$; call it $-\tau N$, which defines $\tau$. For the second, differentiate $N = B \times T$:
$$N' = B' \times T + B \times T' = -\tau\, N \times T + \kappa\, B \times N = \tau B - \kappa T,$$
using $N \times T = -B$ and $B \times N = -T$ for a right-handed orthonormal frame.

For the formula, use $\alpha' = vT$ and $\alpha'' = v'T + \kappa v^2 N$ from above. Differentiating once more, the only part of $\alpha'''$ along $B$ comes from $\kappa v^2 \frac{d}{dt}N = \kappa v^3 (-\kappa T + \tau B)$, so $\alpha''' \cdot B = \kappa \tau v^3$. Since $\alpha' \times \alpha'' = \kappa v^3 B$,
$$(\alpha' \times \alpha'') \cdot \alpha''' = \kappa^2 \tau v^6 = \tau\, |\alpha' \times \alpha''|^2.$$

blocks.title: Helix and twisted cubic
blocks.body: Compute $\kappa$ and $\tau$ for the helix $\alpha(t) = (a\cos t, a\sin t, bt)$ with $a > 0$, and for the twisted cubic $\gamma(t) = (t, t^2, t^3)$ at $t = 0$.
blocks.solution:
Helix. $\alpha' = (-a\sin t, a\cos t, b)$, $\alpha'' = (-a\cos t, -a\sin t, 0)$, $\alpha''' = (a\sin t, -a\cos t, 0)$. Then
$$\alpha' \times \alpha'' = (ab\sin t, -ab\cos t, a^2), \qquad |\alpha' \times \alpha''| = a\sqrt{a^2 + b^2},$$
and $(\alpha' \times \alpha'') \cdot \alpha''' = a^2 b$. With $|\alpha'| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}$,
$$\kappa = \frac{a\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}{(a^2+b^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{a}{a^2+b^2}, \qquad \tau = \frac{a^2 b}{a^2(a^2+b^2)} = \frac{b}{a^2+b^2}.$$
Both are constant, as they must be: a screw motion (rotation about the axis combined with translation along it) maps the helix to itself and moves any point of it to any other. For $b = 0$ the helix is a circle with $\kappa = 1/a$, $\tau = 0$. For $b > 0$ (a right-handed helix) $\tau > 0$; the mirror image, with $b < 0$, has $\tau < 0$. The normal $N = -(\cos t, \sin t, 0)$ points horizontally straight at the axis.

Twisted cubic at $t = 0$. $\gamma'(0) = (1, 0, 0)$, $\gamma''(0) = (0, 2, 0)$, $\gamma'''(0) = (0, 0, 6)$. Then $\gamma' \times \gamma'' = (0, 0, 2)$, so $\kappa(0) = 2/1 = 2$ and $\tau(0) = (0,0,2)\cdot(0,0,6)/4 = 3$. The frame at the origin is the standard basis: $T = e_1$, $N = e_2$, $B = e_3$.

blocks.title: Fundamental theorem of space curves
blocks.body: Given smooth functions $\kappa(s) > 0$ and $\tau(s)$ on an interval $I$, there is a unit-speed curve $\alpha : I \to \mathbb{R}^3$ with curvature $\kappa$ and torsion $\tau$. Any two such curves differ by a rigid motion of the form $x \mapsto Rx + c$ with $R$ a rotation ($\det R = 1$) and $c$ a vector.

blocks.title: Why curvature and torsion are enough
blocks.body:
The Frenet–Serret equations are a linear system of ordinary differential equations for the nine components of $(T, N, B)$, with coefficients $\kappa$ and $\tau$. Choose any right-handed orthonormal frame at $s_0$. By the existence and uniqueness theorem for linear systems (see [[ode-systems]]), there is a unique solution $(T, N, B)$ on all of $I$; one checks that it stays orthonormal, because the coefficient matrix
$$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & \kappa & 0 \\ -\kappa & 0 & \tau \\ 0 & -\tau & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$
is antisymmetric; this implies, again by uniqueness, that the matrix of dot products of $T, N, B$ stays equal to the identity matrix. Then $\alpha(s) = \alpha(s_0) + \int_{s_0}^s T$ is the curve. Changing the initial frame and point is exactly a rigid motion, which gives uniqueness.

Two special cases have short direct proofs.

1. If $\tau \equiv 0$, the curve is planar. Indeed $B' = 0$, so $B$ is a constant vector, and $\frac{d}{ds}\big[(\alpha(s) - \alpha(s_0)) \cdot B\big] = T \cdot B = 0$; the curve stays in the plane through $\alpha(s_0)$ perpendicular to $B$.
2. If in addition $\kappa$ is a positive constant, the curve is part of a circle of radius $1/\kappa$: the candidate centre $c(s) = \alpha(s) + N(s)/\kappa$ has $c' = T + N'/\kappa = T + (-\kappa T)/\kappa = 0$, so it is a fixed point, and $|\alpha(s) - c| = 1/\kappa$.

For plane curves one extra global fact is worth knowing. If $\alpha$ is a regular simple closed plane curve traversed anticlockwise, the total signed curvature $\int k \, ds$ equals $2\pi$: the tangent turns exactly once (Hopf's rotation theorem, stated here without proof). For closed space curves, Fenchel's theorem (also stated without proof) says $\int \kappa\, ds \ge 2\pi$, with equality only for plane convex curves. Statements of this kind, where an integral of curvature is forced by the shape as a whole, are the one-dimensional ancestors of the [[gauss-bonnet|Gauss–Bonnet theorem]].

- The formula $\kappa = |\alpha''|$ is valid only for unit-speed curves. For the parabola $(t, t^2)$, $|\alpha''| = 2$ everywhere, but the curvature is $2/(1+4t^2)^{3/2}$.
- Curvature of a space curve is never negative. Only plane curves have a signed curvature, and its sign depends on the direction of travel.
- Where $\kappa = 0$, the normal $N$ is undefined and the Frenet frame may jump. The curve $(t, 0, e^{-1/t^2})$ for $t > 0$, $(t, e^{-1/t^2}, 0)$ for $t < 0$ (with $(0,0,0)$ at $t = 0$) is smooth, has $\kappa(0) = 0$, and its osculating plane flips by a right angle at $t = 0$, even though $\tau = 0$ wherever it is defined. So 'zero torsion implies planar' needs $\kappa > 0$.
- Speed is not a geometric quantity; it depends on the parametrisation. Arc length, curvature and torsion (up to the sign conventions above) do not.
- Some books define torsion with the opposite sign, $B' = \tau N$. Check the convention before comparing answers.

On a surface, the curvature vector $\kappa N$ of a curve splits into a part normal to the surface and a part tangent to it. The first gives the normal curvatures of [[surfaces-curvature|the surface]], whose extremes are the principal curvatures; the second is the geodesic curvature, which vanishes along geodesics and enters the [[gauss-bonnet|Gauss–Bonnet theorem]]. Choosing a curve to minimise length or another integral involving curvature is a problem in the [[calculus-of-variations]], and the frame-and-equations method of this page generalises to [[riemannian-geometry]].

1. Show that the curve $\alpha(t) = (\cosh t, \sinh t, t)$ has $\kappa = \tau = 1/(2\cosh^2 t)$.
2. Find the point of the curve $y = e^x$ where the curvature is largest.
3. Prove that if all normal lines of a unit-speed plane curve (the lines through $\alpha(s)$ in the direction $N(s)$) pass through one fixed point, the curve is part of a circle.
4. A car drives at constant speed $20$ m/s round a bend shaped like the parabola $y = x^2/100$ (in metres). What is its sideways acceleration at the vertex?

sources.ref: do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces

checks.python:

s = symbols('s', real=True)
for a, b in [(3, 4), (2, -1), (1, 5)]:
    w = sqrt(a**2 + b**2)
    al = Matrix([a*cos(s/w), a*sin(s/w), b*s/w])
    Tv = al.diff(s); assert simplify(Tv.dot(Tv) - 1) == 0
    k = sqrt(simplify(Tv.diff(s).dot(Tv.diff(s))))

entry.sum: At each point of a smooth surface in space, the curvatures of the curves cut out by planes through the normal range between two extremes $k_1 \le k_2$, the principal curvatures. Their product $K = k_1 k_2$ is the Gaussian curvature and their average $H = (k_1 + k_2)/2$ the mean curvature; Gauss's Theorema Egregium says that $K$ depends only on distances measured within the surface, so it cannot be changed by bending without stretching.
key: I = E\,du^2 + 2F\,du\,dv + G\,dv^2, \qquad II = e\,du^2 + 2f\,du\,dv + g\,dv^2
K = k_1 k_2 = \frac{eg - f^2}{EG - F^2}, \qquad H = \frac{k_1 + k_2}{2} = \frac{eG - 2fF + gE}{2(EG - F^2)}
entry.why: Gaussian curvature explains why no flat map of the Earth can keep all distances correct, why a slice of pizza held curled along its width stays stiff lengthwise, and why soap films (mean curvature zero) and bubbles (constant mean curvature) take the shapes they do.

links.note: The pressure difference across a soap bubble or a liquid interface is proportional to its mean curvature (the Young–Laplace law), so equilibrium films with equal pressure on both sides are surfaces with $H = 0$.
A graph $z = h(x,y)$ has mean curvature zero exactly when $h$ satisfies the minimal surface equation $(1 + h_y^2) h_{xx} - 2 h_x h_y h_{xy} + (1 + h_x^2) h_{yy} = 0$, a nonlinear elliptic PDE.

For a graph $z = h(x,y)$ with a critical point at the origin, the Gaussian curvature there is $h_{xx} h_{yy} - h_{xy}^2$, the determinant of the Hessian, so the second-derivative test is a statement about the sign of $K$.
